# Donald Trump Becomes First Ex-US President To Be Found Guilty of a Crime  
In a historic and unprecedented turn of events, **Donald Trump** has become the first former President of the United States to be convicted of a crime. This news has sent shockwaves across the nation and around the world, igniting discussions about the implications for American politics and the legacy of Trump's presidency.
## A Historic Conviction  
The conviction of Donald Trump marks a significant moment in American history. Never before has a former president faced criminal charges, let alone been convicted. The charges against Trump stem from his business dealings and alleged financial misconduct during his time as a real estate mogul and later as President.
## The Charges and Trial  
Trump faced multiple charges, including fraud, **tax evasion**, and obstruction of justice. The case was built around allegations that he had engaged in deceptive financial practices, misrepresented the value of his assets, and evaded taxes over several years. The trial, which garnered massive media attention, included testimonies from former associates, financial experts, and other key witnesses. Throughout the trial, Trump's legal team maintained his innocence, arguing that the charges were politically motivated and that he had always acted within the bounds of the law. However, the jury found sufficient evidence to convict him on several counts, leading to this historic verdict.

results.content:
As Presidents’ Day approaches, it’s not only a time to celebrate the leaders who have shaped our nation, but also a time to reflect on our former Presidents and the legal challenges they faced. Throughout history, presidents have navigated complex legal landscapes, often finding themselves at the center of controversies and facing scrutiny from the public, Congress, and even the courts.  
Most recently, former president, Donald Trump, received four indictments in 2023, making [history](https://www.npr.org/2023/04/05/1168256845/donald-trump-becomes-the-first-president-charged-with-criminal-activity) as the first and only former president to ever be indicted. Other past presidents faced their own political scandals, with some coming close to facing criminal charges. For example, Bill Clinton lied under oath while being deposed for a civil lawsuit. While President Clinton never faced any criminal charges, he was impeached for [perjury](https://bkdefense.com/he-lied-but-is-it-perjury). Another example is Richard Nixon, who became the centerpiece in the infamous Watergate Scandal during his presidency. The scandal involved [burglaries](https://bkdefense.com/robbery-burglary-and-theft-oh-my), illegal wiretaps, and other crimes committed for the advancement of President Nixon’s election campaign. Before President Nixon could be impeached, he resigned and was granted a blanket pardon by his successor, President Gerald Ford, never to face criminal charges.
The first and only sitting president to ever be arrested was Ulysses Grant. In 1872, President Grant was pulled over by [Officer West](https://www.blackpast.org/african-american-history/people-african-american-history/william-henry-west-1842-1915/) for [speeding](https://bkdefense.com/minnesota-traffic-violation-lawyer) in a horse-drawn carriage. President Grant apologized, pledging to follow the regulated speed, and Officer West let him off with a warning. President Grant’s promise did not last long. The very next day, he was caught speeding again by none other than Officer West. Officer West arrested President Grant, who then commended Officer West for [his fearless commitment to his duty](https://www.grantcottage.org/blog/2018/5/18/the-thin-blue-line).

results.name: US: International Context for Prosecuting Former Presidents | Freedom House
results.content:
# US: International Context for Prosecuting Former Presidents  
Legal cases against former heads of state are commonplace in healthy democracies. The United States, with its strong rule-of-law tradition and independent judicial institutions, is entirely capable of handling this challenge and affirming that former presidents are not above the law. Its democracy could even emerge stronger as a result.  
With former president Donald Trump facing criminal charges in four separate federal and state cases, much has been said about the “unprecedented” nature of this moment for American democracy. The observation is true in a narrow sense: never before has a US president or former president been criminally indicted, even if a few[came very close](https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/indictment_of_presidents).
**A common challenge—and opportunity—for democracies**  
Indictments of current and former political leaders are relatively common even in the strongest democracies. Forty-three percent of the world’s freest countries have seen their presidents or prime ministers charged with crimes since 2000.*So it is simply false to claim, as former president Trump and his allies have, that criminal indictments against a former president somehow make the United States a “[third-world nation](https://www.businessinsider.com/trump-allies-fbi-raid-third-world-other-democracies-prosecute-ex-leaders-2022-8)” or a “[banana republic](https://www.washingtontimes.com/news/2023/sep/17/donald-trump-calls-criminal-charges-against-him-ba/).” In fact, some of America’s richest and most established democratic partners have charged current or former leaders in recent decades, including France, Germany, Austria, Portugal, and Italy. The same goes for at least 30 other democracies across five continents, from Israel and Argentina to South Korea and South Africa.  
Still, some argue that the timing of the indictments against Trump, while he is a presidential candidate, makes them uniquely concerning, more akin to the election-rigging tactics of an autocrat than something democracies should be doing. America’s legal institutions also have deep experience with criminal charges against senior political figures. While the United States had technically never indicted a former president before last year, the DOJ has[managed](https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/indictment_of_presidents) multiple criminal investigations and potential prosecutions of presidents and vice presidents. Examples from recent decades include those of Vice President Spiro Agnew, who pleaded “no contest” to tax evasion in exchange for the dropping of corruption charges; President Richard Nixon, whose impending indictment led his successor, President Gerald Ford, to pardon him; and President Bill Clinton, who was ultimately not indicted by an independent counsel.  
More broadly, law enforcement authorities and courts have credibly handled hundreds of investigations and prosecutions of politicians, often for crimes related to corruption and abuse of power. These have resulted in some[35 criminal convictions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_American_federal_politicians_convicted_of_crimes) of federal officials from both major parties since 2001. Other cases have resulted in acquittals, reversals, or reductions in sentences on appeal, as the independent justice process has played out. Most recently, the DOJ under a Democratic administration last year indicted Senator Bob Menendez, a powerful member of the Democratic Party, on a range of corruption-related charges. A trial is set to begin in mid-May.
